title: CBSE Class 12 Accountancy · Practice paper 1
subject: Accountancy
label: Practice paper

secNames.A: Accounting for Partnership Firms and Companies

instr: This question paper contains 34 questions. All questions are compulsory.
This question paper is divided into two parts, Part A and Part B.
Part A (Accounting for Partnership Firms and Companies) is compulsory for all candidates.
In the board paper, Part B has two options: (i) Analysis of Financial Statements and (ii) Computerised Accounting. This practice paper gives Option I, Analysis of Financial Statements.
Questions 1 to 16 and 27 to 30 carry 1 mark each.
Questions 17 to 20, 31 and 32 carry 3 marks each.
Questions 23 to 26 and 34 carry 6 marks each. Question 24 is a case-based question with six sub-parts of 1 mark each (multiple choice in the board paper; short answers here).
Internal choices of the board paper are not included: each question has one version.
This is a practice paper written in the pattern of the CBSE Sample Question Paper 2026-27. It is not an official CBSE paper.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: Kiran, a partner, withdrew ₹6,000 at the beginning of each quarter during the year ended 31st March 2026. The partnership deed allows interest on drawings @ 10% p.a. The interest on Kiran's drawings will be:
questions.sol: Drawings made at the beginning of each quarter carry interest for an average period of 7.5 months. Total drawings = ₹24,000. Interest = 24,000 × 10/100 × 7.5/12 = ₹1,500.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: P, Q and R are partners sharing profits and losses in the ratio of 2 : 2 : 1. R is guaranteed a minimum profit of ₹60,000 a year, and any deficiency is to be borne by P and Q in the ratio of 3 : 2. The firm's profit for the year ended 31st March 2026 was ₹2,00,000. P's share of profit after meeting the guarantee will be:

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text:
Read the following statements, Assertion (A) and Reason (R), and choose the correct option.
Assertion (A): Securities premium received on the issue of shares cannot be used by a company to pay dividend to its shareholders.
Reason (R): Section 52 of the Companies Act, 2013 lists the purposes for which securities premium may be used, and payment of dividend is not one of them.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is correct explanation to (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not correct explanation of (A).
questions.sol: Both statements are true. Securities premium can be used only for the purposes allowed by Section 52 (for example, issue of fully paid bonus shares, writing off preliminary expenses or discount/loss on issue of debentures, premium on redemption, buy-back). Dividend is not among them, which is exactly why (A) holds.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: Neel Ltd. invited applications for 40,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, payable ₹3 on application, ₹4 on allotment and ₹3 on first and final call. Applications were received for 60,000 shares and shares were allotted to all applicants on a pro-rata basis. Excess application money was adjusted towards allotment. How much will be received on allotment from Mohan, who had applied for 1,500 shares?
questions.sol: Mohan is allotted 1,500 × 40,000/60,000 = 1,000 shares. He paid 1,500 × 3 = ₹4,500 on application against ₹3,000 required, so ₹1,500 is excess. Allotment due = 1,000 × 4 = ₹4,000; amount received = 4,000 − 1,500 = ₹2,500.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: X, Y and Z are partners sharing profits in the ratio of 5 : 3 : 2. From 1st April 2026 they decide to share profits in the ratio of 2 : 3 : 5. Which of the following is correct?
options: X sacrifices 3/10, Y gains 1/10 and Z gains 2/10
questions.sol: Old share − new share: X = 5/10 − 2/10 = 3/10 (sacrifice); Y = 3/10 − 3/10 = 0 (no change); Z = 2/10 − 5/10 = −3/10 (gain of 3/10).

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: M and N are partners sharing profits in the ratio of 3 : 2 with capitals of ₹2,40,000 and ₹1,60,000 respectively (after all adjustments). They admit O for 1/5th share in profits. O brings ₹1,20,000 as his capital but nothing for goodwill. The hidden goodwill of the firm is:
questions.sol: Total capital of the firm on the basis of O's share = 1,20,000 × 5/1 = ₹6,00,000. Actual combined capital = 2,40,000 + 1,60,000 + 1,20,000 = ₹5,20,000. Hidden goodwill = 6,00,000 − 5,20,000 = ₹80,000.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: P, Q and R are partners sharing profits in the ratio of 4 : 3 : 2. Q retires, and P and R decide to share future profits in the ratio of 5 : 4. The gaining ratio of P and R is:
questions.sol: Old shares: P = 4/9, R = 2/9. New shares: P = 5/9, R = 4/9. Gain: P = 1/9, R = 2/9. Gaining ratio = 1 : 2.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: On the dissolution of a firm, Ravi, a partner, took over stock of book value ₹50,000 at 10% less than book value. The journal entry for this will be:
options: Ravi's Capital A/c Dr. ₹45,000; To Realisation A/c ₹45,000
Realisation A/c Dr. ₹45,000; To Ravi's Capital A/c ₹45,000
Ravi's Capital A/c Dr. ₹50,000; To Stock A/c ₹50,000
Realisation A/c Dr. ₹5,000; To Ravi's Capital A/c ₹5,000
questions.sol: Stock has already been transferred to the Realisation Account at book value. When a partner takes over an asset, his capital account is debited and the Realisation Account credited with the agreed value, 50,000 − 10% = ₹45,000.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: Gopal Ltd. issued equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹3 per share. The first and final call of ₹4 per share was not paid on 500 shares, and these shares were forfeited. Application and allotment money (including premium) had been received on them. The amount credited to Share Forfeiture Account will be:
questions.sol: Amount received towards share capital on each share = 10 − 4 = ₹6 (the premium was received and stays in Securities Premium). Share Forfeiture A/c is credited with 500 × 6 = ₹3,000.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: Sagar Ltd. purchased machinery for ₹4,50,000 and paid the vendor by issuing 9% debentures of ₹100 each at a premium of 25%. The number of debentures issued will be:
questions.sol: Issue price of one debenture = 100 + 25 = ₹125. Number of debentures = 4,50,000/125 = 3,600.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: Raj Ltd. forfeited 1,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, ₹8 called up, on which the holder had paid ₹5 per share. Out of these, 600 shares were reissued at ₹7 per share as ₹8 paid up. The amount transferred to Capital Reserve will be:
questions.sol: Amount forfeited on the 600 reissued shares = 600 × 5 = ₹3,000. Discount on reissue = 600 × (8 − 7) = ₹600. Capital Reserve = 3,000 − 600 = ₹2,400. (Forfeited amount on the other 400 shares stays in Share Forfeiture A/c.)

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: On the dissolution of a partnership firm, which of the following is debited to the Realisation Account?
options: Cash received from sale of assets
questions.sol: Payment to creditors is recorded as Realisation A/c Dr. To Cash/Bank A/c. A partner's loan is paid by debiting the Partner's Loan A/c, cash from assets sold is credited to Realisation A/c, and accumulated profits are credited to partners' capital accounts.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: There is no partnership deed. On 1st October 2025, partner Vimal gave a loan of ₹50,000 to the firm. The interest payable to Vimal on this loan for the year ended 31st March 2026 will be:
questions.sol: In the absence of a deed, the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 allows interest on a partner's loan @ 6% p.a. For 6 months: 50,000 × 6/100 × 6/12 = ₹1,500. It is a charge against profits.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text:
Orbit Ltd. invited applications for 50,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹2 per share, payable as follows:
On application: ₹5 (including premium ₹2)
On allotment: ₹3
On first and final call: ₹4
Applications were received for 75,000 shares. Applications for 5,000 shares were rejected and their money refunded. The remaining applicants were allotted shares on a pro-rata basis, and excess application money was adjusted towards allotment.
Hari, who had applied for 1,400 shares, paid the application money on all 1,400 shares; his excess application money was adjusted towards allotment, but he did not pay the balance of the allotment money or the call money. His shares were forfeited after the call. Later, all the forfeited shares were reissued at ₹8 per share as fully paid up.
Pass the necessary journal entries in the books of Orbit Ltd. (Calls in Arrears Account is not maintained.)
questions.model:
Working notes: Pro-rata ratio = 50,000 : 70,000 = 5 : 7. Hari is allotted 1,400 × 5/7 = 1,000 shares. He paid 1,400 × 5 = ₹7,000 on application against ₹5,000 due on 1,000 shares, so ₹2,000 is excess adjusted towards allotment; allotment unpaid = 1,000 × 3 − 2,000 = ₹1,000. The premium was payable with application and Hari paid it, so Securities Premium is not debited on forfeiture. Total excess application money = 20,000 × 5 = ₹1,00,000; allotment received = 1,50,000 − 1,00,000 − 1,000 = ₹49,000.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: In the Balance Sheet of a company, 'Calls in advance' is shown under the sub-head:
questions.sol: Calls in advance (with interest accrued on it) is money received before it is called; it is a liability of the company, shown under Current Liabilities, sub-head Other Current Liabilities. It is not part of share capital.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text:
Read the following statements, Assertion (A) and Reason (R), and choose the correct option.
Assertion (A): Purchase of inventory for cash reduces the quick ratio.
Reason (R): Inventory is not included in quick (liquid) assets.
options: Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is incorrect
A is incorrect but R is correct
questions.sol: Cash, a quick asset, goes down while inventory, which is not a quick asset, goes up; current liabilities do not change. So quick assets fall and the quick ratio falls. This happens only because inventory is excluded from quick assets, so R explains A.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: For a company that is not a financial enterprise, which of the following is a cash flow from financing activities?
questions.sol: Dividend paid is a financing activity. Interest received by a non-financial company and purchase of goodwill are investing activities; income tax paid is normally an operating activity.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: The net book value of machinery was ₹5,00,000 at the beginning of the year and ₹6,20,000 at the end of the year. Depreciation charged for the year was ₹60,000. Machinery with a book value of ₹40,000 was sold during the year at a profit of ₹10,000. The amount of machinery purchased during the year is:
questions.sol: Purchases = Closing book value + Depreciation + Book value of machinery sold − Opening book value = 6,20,000 + 60,000 + 40,000 − 5,00,000 = ₹2,20,000. (The profit on sale does not affect the machinery account at book value.)

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text:
The current assets of a company are ₹4,00,000 and its current liabilities are ₹2,00,000. State, with reason, whether each of the following transactions (taken separately) will increase, decrease or not change the current ratio:
(i) Goods costing ₹50,000 were purchased on credit.
(ii) A computer (fixed asset) with a book value of ₹20,000 was sold for ₹20,000 in cash.
(iii) ₹30,000 was received from a debtor.
(iv) A bill payable of ₹40,000 was paid by cheque.
questions.model:
Present current ratio = 4,00,000/2,00,000 = 2 : 1
(i) Decrease. Current assets and current liabilities both rise by ₹50,000: 4,50,000/2,50,000 = 1.8 : 1. When the ratio is more than 1, an equal increase in both lowers it.
(ii) Increase. Cash (a current asset) rises by ₹20,000 and current liabilities do not change: 4,20,000/2,00,000 = 2.1 : 1.
(iii) No change. One current asset (cash) rises and another (debtors) falls by the same amount; total current assets stay ₹4,00,000.
(iv) Increase. Current assets and current liabilities both fall by ₹40,000: 3,60,000/1,60,000 = 2.25 : 1.

points.t: (i) Decrease, with reason (both rise equally; 1.8 : 1)
(ii) Increase, with reason (only current assets rise; 2.1 : 1)
(iii) No change, with reason (one current asset replaces another)
(iv) Increase, with reason (both fall equally; 2.25 : 1)
